claims.text: The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has superior strain hardening to its equiatomic quaternary and ternary FCC subsets.
The quinary alloy fails later than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Greater compositional complexity in the quinary alloy produces stronger local lattice distortion.
Greater compositional complexity promotes development of chemical short-range order during thermomechanical processing.
Increasing the number of constituents creates a richer diversity of local bonding or atomic-pair environments.
Local lattice distortion acts as a barrier to dislocation motion.
Chemical short-range order raises barriers to dislocation activity.
The proposed dislocation barriers cause an earlier onset of strain hardening in the quinary alloy.
The proposed dislocation barriers cause a greater strain-hardening magnitude in the quinary alloy.
The proposed dislocation barriers delay failure in the quinary alloy.
The quinary alloy will exhibit broader high-resolution XRD peaks as evidence of enhanced lattice distortion.
The quinary alloy will exhibit more distinct short-range-order signatures detectable by atom probe tomography.
Lattice-distortion and short-range-order signatures will correlate with earlier and greater strain hardening.
Differences in stacking-fault energy may influence the deformation behavior of the compared alloys.
Stacking-fault energy influences activation of dislocation slip, twinning, and martensitic transformation.

contradictions.description: The controls call for identical initial microstructural conditions, while the hypothesis says composition-dependent CSRO develops during thermomechanical processing and should differ before testing. This is inconsistent unless 'identical microstructure' is explicitly restricted to grain size and dislocation density rather than local chemical order and lattice distortion.
